summary: Surviving in Mars is an interactive simulator that places players in charge of a Martian outpost. Players make decisions to keep the outpost running while balancing essential mission needs such as life support, power and ratiation protection. The game addresses the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge by turning these competing demands into a hands-on experience: players can see how resource choices affect the outpost and the success of its mission. This project is important because it makes the engineering trade-offs of living on Mars accessible to young learners and encourages them to think like mission planners. details:
What does it do ?

Surviving in Mars is a mission-management simulator about operating a Martian outpost. It is designed to help young players explore how life support, power, food production, radiation protection, and local resources affect one another. Players make mission decisions and see how limited resources and environmental conditions can influence the outpost and the mission’s chances of success.

[surviving in mars main menu and gameplay pictures]

How does it work and what benefits does it have ?

The game is supported by a data pipeline that collects, preserves, standardizes, and packages selected data for local use. The pipeline includes weather feeds for NASA’s Curiosity and Perseverance rovers; InSight TWINS wind data; Mars dust-opacity and radiation measurements; solar events from NASA’s DONKI database; MOLA topography; Mars reference facts; and NASA technical references on crew needs, life support, agriculture, power systems, in-situ resource use, and radiation shielding. It organizes selected information into local database tables, JSON data, and raster map products, with source information retained for traceability. This approach allows the web game to use a prepared local data package without relying on a live NASA connection during every play session.

The project’s benefit is that it turns space exploration concepts into decisions players can explore. Instead of presenting Mars survival only as facts, the simulator encourages systems thinking: a choice that helps one part of the outpost may place pressure on another. Its intended impact is to build curiosity about space science and engineering, and to help young learners understand why planning a real mission involves trade-offs.

A key factor in development was scientific transparency. The collected datasets come from different missions, locations, time periods, and measurement systems, so they cannot automatically be treated as simultaneous observations of one outpost. The project also distinguishes measured data from simplified game values. For example, RAD measurements are detector readings rather than a direct measure of human health risk, and ice-consistency maps are evidence maps rather than estimates of extractable water. The simulator is an educational model, not a validated engineering design for a Mars habitat.

What is the intended impact of the project ?

Surviving in Mars aims to strengthen scientific literacy, problem-solving, and decision-making skills among children aged 7–12. By managing life support, energy, and radiation protection, players can explore how scientific and engineering choices affect a mission’s survival. The simulator encourages learners to test strategies, observe consequences, and adapt their decisions, helping them connect scientific concepts to practical challenges. It also aims to support educators with an interactive resource for scientific inquiry and encourage lasting curiosity about science, engineering, and space exploration

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did we use to develop our project?

Assets tools

  • Audio: Itch.io;
  • 2D Models: Itch.io;
  • Images: Pinterest, PineTools Pixelize, ChatGPT.

Development tools

  • Data collection and pipeline: Python, SQLite, JSON and raster data;
  • Web game: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, NodeJS, GoDaddy domain;
  • AI tools: Codex and Copilot as a coding assistant and ChatGPT for research, writing and image generation;
  • Design and collaboration: Figma, Google Docs, Discord, Git, VS Code.
